title: "max" and "all" produce a single result based on multiple values.
body: max and all reduce an iterable to one result. max returns the largest item but raises ValueError for an empty iterable; all tests whether every item is truthy and returns True for an empty iterable. Distinguish an item result from a Boolean result and consider empty input.
when_to_show: This is demonstrated in the beginner-level built-in function card that covers `max()`, `all()`, maximum values, and whether all conditions are met.

title: `extend` and `insert` are methods that directly modify a list.
body: Both `extend()` and `insert()` are methods that directly modify the state of a list. `extend(other)` iterates through the elements in `other` one by one and appends them to the end of the list. Therefore, `items.extend([3, 4])` does not insert a single list named `[3, 4]`, but rather adds 3 and 4 individually. This is the key difference from `append([3, 4])`. `insert(index, value)` inserts `value` before the specified position. For example, `insert(1, 'x')` inserts the new value at index 1, and the existing elements are shifted to the right. For beginners, the modified list itself is more important than the return value. These methods typically return `None` and modify the original list. When working with ordered data—such as a list of cards, a list of files, or validation steps—you must understand `extend` and `insert` to avoid nested lists or ordering errors. When tracing code, comparing the list before the method call, the value being added, and the list after the call in a table format helps you understand it more quickly. Comparing `append`, `extend`, and `insert` together allows you to read code that modifies lists more reliably. `append` adds a single value to the end, `extend` appends multiple values, and `insert` inserts a value before a specified position. Since all three methods directly modify the original list, storing the return value in a variable—such as `result = items.extend(...)`—may result in `None`. A common mistake made by beginners is failing to distinguish between `extend` and `append`, which can lead to nested lists. Additionally, since `insert` shifts the positions of subsequent elements as values are added to the front, it can affect the following code that uses indices. To verify your code, try writing down the list before the call, the values passed, and the list after the call; this can help reduce bugs.
when_to_show: This is demonstrated in problems involving adding multiple values to a list or inserting values in the middle of a list.
detail: `extend` and `insert` are methods that directly modify a list. `extend([3, 4])` does not add an entire list; instead, it appends 3 and 4 to the end of the list, respectively. `insert(index, value)` inserts a value before the specified position, pushing the subsequent elements to the right. You must specify the list before the call, the value to be added, and the list after the call.

title: raise, TypeError, and KeyError are signals that reveal failures rather than hiding them
body: `raise` is a statement that causes the code to throw an exception directly. It explicitly signals a failure—such as `raise ValueError(...)`—when a value is incorrect or when continuing would cause a more serious problem. A `TypeError` often occurs when a value’s type or usage is incorrect. For example, you should suspect a `TypeError` if you add a string and a number directly or pass a data type that a function does not expect. A `KeyError` often occurs when you try to access a key that does not exist in a dictionary using square brackets. If `age` is not present in JSON or an API response but you try to access it as `user['age']`, a `KeyError` may occur. For beginners, it’s more important to learn the verification steps indicated by the error than to memorize the error names. For a `TypeError`, first check, “Is the data type of this value correct?” For a `KeyError`, check, “Does this key actually exist in this dictionary?” And for a `raise`, check, “Was the code intentionally made to stop here?” In validation scripts, the pattern of using `raise` to halt execution is often used to prevent silently producing incorrect results. When analyzing exceptions, look separately at the error name, the error message, and the line where the error occurred. `raise` indicates that the coder intentionally caused a failure, while `TypeError` and `KeyError` may be issues Python detected during execution. A TypeError doesn’t always mean that a simple type conversion will fix it. A TypeError can also occur if too many arguments are passed to a function, if `None` is called as if it were a function, or if a list and a number are added incorrectly. Similarly, a KeyError may not be a problem that can be solved simply by changing the code to use `get`. If a key is required, there was an error in the data creation process; if a key is optional, a default value should be specified. Therefore, exception handling is not a technique for hiding errors, but a procedure for identifying where the agreement between the data and the code was broken.
when_to_show: This is shown on the card that asks about exception types, direct errors, dict key errors, and data type errors.
detail: `raise` is a statement that explicitly signals a failure in the code, and the error type indicates the cause of the problem. `TypeError` typically occurs due to data type or usage issues, `KeyError` occurs when attempting to access a key that doesn’t exist in a dictionary, and `ValueError` often results from a failed value conversion. Rather than hiding errors, these should be viewed as signals that clearly indicate where and why the program stopped.

title: A traceback starts with the last line of the error and reads back from the line of code immediately above it.
body: A traceback is a log that shows the path through which Python encountered an error. It might look intimidating at first, but as a beginner, you just need to follow a specific order when reading it. First, look at the last line. The last line usually displays the error type—such as KeyError, TypeError, or ValueError—along with a brief message. Next, look at the line of code immediately above it. That line is likely where the error actually occurred. Then, check the filename and line number to locate the specific file and line in question. Trying to translate the entire traceback from the top down takes a long time, but by looking at the last error line and the code line immediately above it first, you can quickly narrow down the scope of the problem. If it’s a KeyError: 'age', check if you’re trying to access a key that doesn’t exist; if it’s a TypeError, verify that the data type is correct. Debugging is not about guesswork; it’s the process of systematically connecting error messages, line numbers, and actual values. When reading a traceback, don’t stop at just the last line—formulate a hypothesis based on that line, then go back to the line immediately above it to verify it. For example, if you see a `KeyError: 'age'`, hypothesize that the `age` key is missing, and check the line immediately above to see which dictionary is accessing `['age']`. If you encounter a `TypeError`, you can print the data types of the values on both sides of an operator or the arguments passed to a function. If you encounter a `FileNotFoundError`, check both the path string and the current working directory. Since long tracebacks contain multiple layers of function calls, understand that the very bottom line indicates the actual point of the error, while the lines above it represent the call path leading up to that point. If you include the error type, filename, line number, suspected values, and verification commands in your debugging notes, you’ll be able to resolve the issue much faster if the same error recurs.
when_to_show: This is shown on a card that asks about error logs, tracebacks, and the debugging process.
detail: A traceback is a log that shows the path where an error occurred. Even if it’s long, start by looking at the error type and message on the last line, then check the filename, line number, and actual code line immediately above it. If it’s a KeyError, check for a missing key; if it’s a TypeError, check the data type; if it’s a ValueError, check the conversion value—and narrow down the issue by printing the actual values.

title: assert and pytest help you develop the habit of comparing expected values with actual values
body: assert is useful for internal assumptions and test expectations, while pytest collects tests that follow its discovery rules. Python optimization can remove assert statements, so never rely on them for required user-input validation or production behavior. Passing tests guarantee only the cases and properties that were written.
when_to_show: This is shown on a card that asks about assert, pytest, expected/actual, regression testing, and verification routines.
